senses.def: When you point a weapon at people or things, you aim it at them.
ex: The robber aimed the gun right at me.
He was aiming the arrow at the apple, but he missed.

senses.def: When you aim at something you want, you do what is necessary to get it.
ex: The manager said she was aiming at a 14 percent increase in sales next year.
The new law is aimed at reducing crime in the streets.

senses.def: When you do something designed to affect one class or type of people, you aim it at those people.
When you ask for something, you tell someone that you want it.
ex: We asked the waiter for some more coffee.
My wife might ask for more vacation time instead of a raise.

senses.def: When you say that people are asking for something or asking for it, you mean that they are doing or saying something that is likely to result in punish- ment or a negative consequence.
ex: I'm warning you - if you keep doing that, you're asking for trouble.
You're asking for it! Don't say that again.

senses.def: When you ask people out, you ask them to go with you to a place of entertainment in order to have fun and spend time together.
ex: Being asked out by Tom was quite a surprise to Judy.

senses.def: When one side in a disagreement stops making threats and lets the other have what it wants or do what it wants, the side that stops making threats backs down.
ex: The dictator didn't back down after nited Nations Security Council voted in favor of sending in troops.
The police officer tried to force me to pay him a bribe, but when I said I would report him to the chief of police, he backed down.

senses.def: When you move away from danger or a person you are arguing or fighting with in order to avoid injury or a more serious fight or argument, you back off. When you tell people to back off, you are warning them that you are becoming angry and that a fight or argument is likely.
ex: I'm warning you! You'd better back off.
Tom backed off when he saw that Jake had a gun.

senses.def: When you walk backward, you back up. When you drive a vehicle in reverse, you back up or back the vehicle up.
ex: The fire was so hot that we had to back up.
I put the car in reverse and backed it up.

senses.def: When you are explaining something, and you repeat something that you already said, you back up.
ex: You're going too fast. Can you back up a little and explain your plan again?
Sorry, I forgot part of the story. Let me back up a little.

senses.def: When you make a claim or statement and then show people evidenceorgivethem informationprovingthat the claimor statement istrueor correct, you back it up.
ex: No one believed Jim's accusations because he couldn't back them up with any evidence.
The IRS asked me for some receipts to back up my deductions.

senses.def: When you support people in a conflict or a confrontation, you back them up. When you support people by doing some work or a difficult assignment, you back them up.
ex: Linda said she would back me up if I complained about our supervisor.
The general backed up his threats with 400,000 soldiers.
Jerry is the restaurant's main cook, and Tanya backs him up when it gets busy.

senses.def: When you duplicate important information, such as a computer program or data, so that you will still have it if the original information is lost or damaged, you back it up.
ex: If you're going to install that new software, be sure you back up your entire hard disk first.
I back my work up every day before I go home.

senses.def: When something backs up, it is being prevented from moving, progressing, or flowing normally.
ex: An accident backed traffic up for three miles.
The assembly line is going to back up if Erik doesn't get the parts he needs soon.

related.def: Someone or something that supports or is ready to provide support in a conflict or a confrontation by doing some work or a difficult assignment is a backup.
ex: When the rioters grew more violent, the police called for backup.
The firefighter entered the burning building without a backup.

related.def: A duplicate of important information, such as a computer program or data, is a backup.
ex: I keep a backup of my important computer files on my other computer.
The major gave a backup copy of the battle plan to his secretary.

related.def: After you duplicate important information, such as a computer phrasal verbs used in compound nouns program or data, the original is backed up.
ex: I accidentally erased your book from your computer. I hope your work was backed up.
The hospital bought a generator to back up nreliable city power supply.
We kept the old computer to back the new one up.

related.def: When a piece of equipment or machinery is very important and another is kept available in case the one that is normally used fails, the second piece of equipment or machinery is a backup.
ex: The skydiver checked his main parachute and his backup before the flight.
The school had to close when the main power and the backup both failed.

related.def: A backup is a situation in which something is being prevented from moving, progressing, or flowing normally.

The huge number of Christmas cards and packages caused a backup at the post office.

related.def: When something is being prevented from moving, progressing, or flowing normally, it is backed up.
ex: Let's take the train downtown. Traffic is always backed up at this time of the morning.

ex: The muggers stole my money and then beat me up.
Timmy got beaten up at school today.

related.def: When something is in bad condition because of heavy use, it is beat-up.
ex: My car is an old, beat-up piece of junk.

senses.def: When you beef up security or some other arrangement to prevent . or deal with a problem, you make this arrangement stronger.
ex: After the terrorist attack, security was beefed up at the embassy.
The hospital decided to beef up its emergency facilities.
The coach is planning to beef the defense up.

senses.def: When you believe in something or believe in doing something, you have a strong opinion about something that is important to you.
ex: I believe in working hard and saving money.
Maria doesn't believe in sex before marriage.

ex: Do you believe in ghosts?
Nedis an atheist. He doesn't believe in God.

senses.def: When you believe in people, you have confidence in them and believe what they say because you think they are honest, correct, or competent.
ex: I don't care what anyone else says, I still believe in you.
We want to believe in you, but we need some proof that your invention really works.

senses.def: When you bite off something, you use your teeth to remove a piece. When you bite off more than you can chew,you agree to do something that , you do not have the time or the ability to do.
ex: The lion bit off a huge piece of the zebra's flesh.

senses.def: When the wind moves something away from where it was, it blows it away.
ex: Don't leave the newspaper outside. The wind will blow it away.
The picnic wasn't much fun. It was really windy, and everything kept blowing away.

senses.label: informal
senses.def: When a person or company has an ability, product, or service that is much better than that of a competing person or company, it blows away the competing person or company.
ex: Apple's new computer is so fast it's going to blow away the competition.
I thought I had a chance to win the race, but Erik just blew me away.

senses.label: informal
senses.def: When something you have seen or heard makes you very shocked, amazed, or emotional, it blows you away.
ex: The first time I saw the Pyramids, they just blew me away.

senses.label: informal
senses.def: When you do not do something that you are supposed to do because you do not want to or because you do not think it is important, you blow it off.
ex: I was supposed to report for jury duty Monday morning, but I blew it off.

senses.def: When a flame blows out or is blown out by a strong wind,it stops burning. When you blow out a flame, you use your breath to make the flame stop burning.
ex: Don't open the window - the candles will blow out.
I couldn't light my cigarette. The wind kept blowing the match out.
The stove isn't working. Maybe the pilot light has blown out.

senses.def: When something is moved outward away from where it was by an explosion or a very strong wind, it is blown out or blown out of where it was before.
ex: The force of the explosion blew all the windows out.
Look, there's a dead bird. The wind might have blown it out of its nest.

senses.def: When a piece of electrical equipment or a fuse blows out, it fails because too much electricity is passing through it.
ex: Don't be surprised if the fuse blows out -- you have seven lights, your computer, and your TV all plugged into one outlet.
When lightning hit our house, it blew all the telephones out.

related.def: When a tire bursts and suddenly loses its air while you are driving, you have a blowout.
ex: Maria had a blowout while she was driving, lost control of her car, and hit a tree.

senses.def: When something blows up or when someone blows something up,it explodes.
ex: Seven people were killed when the building blew up.
The hijackers ultimately blew the plane up.

senses.def: When something blows up or when someone blows something up,it becomes much larger because air or something else is being forced into it.
ex: It always takes me an hour or more to blow up the balloons for a party.
Hank blew up a beach ball and threw it in the pool.

senses.def: When you make a picture or photograph larger, you blow it up.
ex: I blew the photograph up and framed it.
When you blow this photo of the car up, you can make out the license plate number.

senses.def: [informal] When you blow up or blow up at someone, you suddenly become very angry. When you blow up over something, you suddenly become very angry because of it.
ex: Heather blew up when she saw her boyfriend dancing with Linda.
Heather blew up at her boyfriend when she saw him dancing with Linda.

related.def: A blowup is a picture or photograph that has been made larger.
ex: I made a blowup of the photo and framed it.

senses.def: When you say that something boils down to something else, you are saying that it is the basic cause of a more complicated situation or problem.
ex: Most of the crime in this city boils down to drugs.

senses.def: When something mechanical breaks down,it does not function I was late for work because my car broke down. This photocopier is a piece of junk -- it breaks down every day.
When an arrangement, agreement, negotiation, plan,or marriage breaks down, one or more persons involved is not cooperating or participating because of a disagreement or problem.
ex: After he started drinking heavily, their marriage started to break down.
The peace negotiations broke down because neither side was willing to compromise.
Neither side would give an inch, and there was a breakdown in the negotiations.

senses.def: When you break down, you lose self-control and become emotionally or mentally confused.
ex: When the judge sentenced Jones to life in prison, he broke down and begged for mercy.
Tom breaks down whenever he thinks of the tragedy.

senses.def: When something decomposes or reduces to its smallest parts or is reduced by someone to its smallest parts, it breaks down.
ex: After the poison breaks down, it's quite harmless.
Anticoagulant drugs are used to break down blood clots.

senses.def: When you reduce a process, situation, problem, plan, or idea to its basic parts to make it easier to understand, you break it down.
ex: The professor's plan seemed really complicated, but after he broke it down for us, we understood it a little better.
If you break the manufacturing process down into steps, it's easier to train new workers.

senses.def: When you use force to go through a door that is locked, you break it down.
ex: A door had to be broken down to rescue the people trapped by the fire.

related.def: When something is old, in bad condition, or not functioning properly, it is broken-down.
ex: My car is a broken-down piece of junk.

related.def: A breakdown is a situation in which something mechanical has broken down.
ex: After that last breakdown, I decided it was time for a new car.

related.def: A situation in which someone has broken down and is very upset or confused is a breakdown.
ex: Marty had a complete mental breakdown and started to see invisible people.

senses.def: When you break in a new. mechanical device or a car, you use it slowly and carefully until you are sure it ready for heavier use. When you break in a pair of shoes, you wear them only occasionally and for a short time until they are comfortable. When you break in people at a new job, you train and supervise them and give them less than the normal amount of work until they are ready for something more difficult.
ex: I don't want to wear these boots on the expedition. I haven't broken them in yet.
We're breaking in a new secretary, so things have been a bit confused at our office lately.

related.def: After you break in a new mechanical device or a car, a pair of shoes, or people at a new job, they are broken in.
ex: After I arrive in Denver, I'll go straight to my hotel and check in.
Jim checked into the hotel while I called home to check on the kids.

senses.def: When something breaks off or someone breaks something off, a part or smaller piece is separated from something larger by force.
ex: Jim broke off a piece of chocolate and gave it to his girlfriend.
One of the arms broke off the statue when it fell off the pedestal.
The handle of the coffee cup is broken off.

senses.def: When you break off relations or contact with someone, you decide to end relations or contact with that person.
ex: The two countries broke off relations with each other.

senses.def: When you escape from a place where you are a prisoner, you break out or break out of that place.
ex: Kevin broke out of prison last month.
The police have been looking for him ever since he broke out.

senses.def: When fighting begins suddenly, it breaks out.
ex: Rioting broke out after the general canceled the election.

related.def: An escape from prison is a breakout.
ex: There hasn't been a successful breakout from the state prison in more than 25 years.

senses.def: When you use force to go through a wall or other barrier, you break through it.
ex: The thieves broke through the wall of the jewelry store.
The attackers couldn't break through the thick walls of the fort.

senses.def: When you cannot do something because of a problem and you find a way to solve or eliminate the problem, you break through or break through the problem.
ex: After the problem of tissue rejection is broken through, organ transplants will become more common.
It took three days of negotiation, but we finally broke through the deadlock.

senses.def: When you break up a fight, you stop the fight.
ex: Two students were fighting, and the teacher broke them up.
There was no way I could break up the fight between the two dogs.

senses.def: When a gathering of people separates, it breaks up. When the police tell people who are gathered together in a crowd to separate and leave the area, the police break the gathering up.
ex: The meeting should break up around 3:00.
The police ordered the gang members to break it up.
The demonstration was broken up by riot police.

senses.def: When two people end a romantic relationship, they with that person. When other people cause a couple to break up, they break the couple up.
ex: I was sad to hear that Jim and Nancy had broken up.
It was Jim's secretary who broke them up.

senses.def: When something breaks into smaller pieces, it breaks up. When you break something into smaller pieces, you break it up.
ex: The meteor broke up when it entered Earth's atmosphere.
Sally broke the cookie up before giving it to her baby.

senses.def: When something breaks up the day or some other period of time, it interrupts that time and makes it less boring.
ex: The bank guard likes to chat with the tellers once in a while to break up the day.

related.def: When two people end a romantic relationship,a breakup occurs.
ex: Nancy is very upset about the breakup.

related.def: When something breaks into smaller pieces, a breakup takes place.
ex: The breakup of AT&T created several smaller telephone companies.

senses.def: When you take something to another place and then bring it from that place to the place where you were before, you bring it back.
ex: I told Tom to bring my pen right back.
Sally borrowed my blue sweater and brought it back yesterday.

senses.def: When something that was popular or current in the past is introduced again, it is brought back.
ex: Many schools are bringing back uniforms for children.
Every few years designers try to bring miniskirts back.

senses.def: When something causes you to recall memories and emotions from the past, it brings the memories and emotions back.
ex: Looking at these old pictures brought back wonderful memories.

senses.def: When people take something from one place to the place where you are, they bring it over.
ex: I called Frank to ask if I could use his electric drill, and he brought it right over.

senses.def: When people bring something from a higher level or position or from south to north to where you are, they bring it up or bring it up to where you are.
ex: Would you please go downstairs and bring up the package that was just delivered?
The rescue workers brought morphine up to the injured mountain climber.

senses.def: When you introduce a new topic into a conversation,you bring it up.
ex: Last night during dinner, Dad brought up the idea of saving money by staying home instead of taking a vacation this year.
You and your big mouth! We were having a great time until you brought that up.

senses.def: When you bring up children, you care for them as they grow to adulthood. When you bring up children to believe something or to behave in a certain way, you try to teach this belief or behavior to them.
ex: Tom was born in Canada, but he was brought up in nited States.
Bringing quadruplets up is a lot of work.
I was brought up to believe in honesty and compassion.

senses.def: When you brush people off, you ignore them or refuse to listen to them because you are not interested in or do not like what they are saying
ex: My boss just brushes me off when I try to tell her how to increase our profits.
The reporters tried to ask him some questions, but he brushed them off.

senses.def: When you brush off a critical remark or problem, you ignore it and continue as before without letting it affect you.
ex: I told Dr. Smith that he had made a mistake, but he brushed it off.

related.def: When you give people the brush-off, you ignore them or refuse to listen to them because you are not interested in or do not like what they are saying.
ex: The boss just gave me the brush-off when I tried to give him some advice.

senses.def: When you brush up or brush up on something,you study or practice a skill or subject you used to know but have forgotten or partly forgotten.
ex: It's been a long time since I studied algebra, but I'm going to need it if I go back to school to study for my master's degree, so I'd better brush up.
Frank's going to Peru next month, so he's been brushing up on his Spanish.
Welcome to my house. Please come in.
The burglar came into the house through the back door.

senses.def: When you bump into things or people, you accidentally hit them with your body.
ex: I couldn't see where I was going in the dark, and I bumped into the door.
Would you please move these boxes -- I keep bumping into them.

senses.def: When you meet people unexpectedly or unintentionally, you bump into them. Run into is the same as bump into.
ex: We bumped into Sarah at the mall today.

senses.def: When a building or other structure burns down or someone burns it down, it is completely destroyed by fire.
ex: Though most of Chicago burned down in 1871, a few buildings survived.

senses.def: When a fire, candle, or other flame stops burning because it has no more fuel, it burns out.
ex: Don't worry. The sun won't burn out for another four billion years.

senses.def: When a light bulb stops producing light because it has reached the end of its useful life, it burns out.
ex: These new bulbs are guaranteed not to burn out for ten years.
I can't see what I'm doing because this bulb has burned out.

senses.def: When people are forced to leave their home or some other shelter or hiding place because of fire or fire damage, they are burned out
ex: The only way to get the enemy soldiers out of the tunnels was to burn them out.
Seven families were burned out of their homes by the huge fire.

related.def: After a fire, candle, or other flame stops burning because it has no more fuel, it is burned-out.
ex: The burned-out rocket landed in the ocean.

related.def: When people are extremely tired, either physically or psycho- logically, because of stress or hard work, they are burned-out. Teaching those awful students for so many years has left him burned-out. Taking care of four small children day after day would leave any mother burned-out.
A light bulb that no longer produces light because it has reached the end of its useful life is burned-out.
ex: I climbed the ladder and unscrewed the burned-out bulb.

related.def: Something that has been damaged or destroyed by fire is burned-out.
ex: After the war, nothing was left but burned-out cars and buildings.

senses.def: When something is completely destroyed by heat or fire, it burns up.
ex: The meteor burned up in the atmosphere.
The rocket's fuel will burn up after only 40 seconds.

senses.def: When people or things destroy something with heat or fire, they burn it up.
ex: There's no more coal. We burned it all up.
Jet engines burn up fuel at a tremendous rate.

related.def: After something is completely destroyed by heat or fire, it is burned up.
ex: There isn't anymore firewood. It's all burned up.
The house is all burned up. There's no way it can be saved.

senses.def: [informal] When something makes you very angry,it burns you up.
ex: It really burns me up when other people take credit for my work.

related.def: [informal] When you are very angry, you are burned up.
ex: Jim was burned up when his boss criticized him during the meeting.

senses.def: When you burst out laughing or crying, you begin laughing or crying loudly and suddenly.
ex: Heather burst out laughing when I fell into the swimming pool.

ex: I was trying to talk to Jim at the party, but Bob kept butting in.

senses.def: When you leave a place or walk away from a person and are then asked to return, you are called back.

Mike tried to calm his sister down after she had a fight with her husband.

senses.def: When a confused or violent situation becomes less confused or violent, it calms down. When you calm a confused or violent situation down, you make it less confused or violent and more calm. Settle down is similar to calm down.

senses.def: When you carry on, you continue as before, despite a difficult experience in your life.
ex: You'll have to carry on for the sake of the children.
It was difficult for Mrs. Nelson to carry on after her husband died.

senses.def: When you carry on, carry on with an activity, or carry on doing an activity, you continue it or continue doing it.

Before your flight you have to go to the check-in counter.

ex: That bag is too big for carry-on - you'll have to check it in.

senses.def: When you check a place or thing out, you inspect it carefully or learn more about it.
ex: That new Mexican restaurant is great - you should check it out.
Hey George, check out that car Todd is driving. When did he buy it?

senses.def: When you check people out, you investigate them in order mation they have given you about themselves, such as their education and work experience, has been investigated and found to be accurate.

senses.def: When something dries up or something dries it up,all the water or other liquid in it goes away.
ex: The sun came out and dried up all the rain.
The Great Salt Lake is slowly drying up.

senses.def: When the amount or supply of something gets smaller and then disappears completely, it dries up.
ex: The small grocery store's business dried up after a huge supermarket opened across the street.

related.def: After all water or other liquid in something goes away,it is dried up.
ex: These leaves will burn now that they're dried up.

senses.def: When you eat food up, you eat all of it.
ex: There's no more pizza. David ate it all up.
Don't eat up the cake before your father gets a piece.

senses.def: When something eats up something else, such as money or time, it uses all of it.
ex: I'm broke. Fixing my car last week ate up my entire paycheck.

forms: phrasal verbs with the particle out

senses.def: When you completely remove the contents of a space or container, you empty it out.
ex: The police officer told me to empty out my pockets.
After we empty this room out, we can start painting.

senses.def: When all the people in a place leave it, the place empties out.
ex: After the concert is over, it'll be 20 minutes before the auditorium empties out.

related.def: After the contents of a container have been completely removed, the container is emptied out.
ex: Now that the room is emptied out, we can start laying the carpet.

senses.def: When people end up doing something or end up a certain way, it is the result of a series of decisions, actions, or unplanned and unexpected occurrences. End up is similar to wind up.
ex: A hurricane was approaching Florida, so we ended up coming home from our vacation early.
Judy has never gone skydiving before, so she'll probably end up in the hospital with two broken legs.

senses.def: When people or things end up in a place,this place is where their journey ends even though the outcome may have been unplanned or unexpected.
ex: How did London Bridge end up in Arizona?
The taxi driver didn't understand me, and we ended up in Newark instead of New York.

senses.def: When the parts of something become completely separated because it is old or in bad condition, it falls apart.
ex: These old shoes are starting to fall apart.
There's no way to fix this thing. It has completely fallen apart.

senses.def: When a plan, arrangement, system, or agreement fails, it falls apart.
ex: After five difficult years, their marriage totally fell apart.
The peace agreement is slowly falling apart.

senses.def: When people suddenly lose control and start laughing or become very upset or emotional, they fall apart.
ex: Sally fell apart when she heard the tragic news.

senses.def: When you are in a group that is walking, running, driving, and so on, and they move ahead of you because you are moving more slowly than the oth- ers, you fall behind. Keep up is the opposite of fall behind.
ex: Keith and Tom are walking so fast that I've fallen behind.
I was supposed to be following Linda to the party, but I fell behind and got lost.

senses.def: When you are in a group that is studying, working, and so on, and they learn faster or get more work done because you are learning or working more slowly than the others, you fall behind or fall behind in your work, studies, and so on. When you do not complete work as fast as it was originally planned and expected, you fall behind schedule. Get behind is similar to fall behind. Keep up is the opposite of fall behind.
ex: Timmy was sick last semester, and he fell behind in his studies.
The sales manager wanted to know why I had fallen behind the rest of the department.
The building project will fall behind schedule if the construction workers go on strike.

senses.def: When you do not make the regular payments you are required to make, you fall behind or fall behind in your payments.
ex: When I lost my job, I fell behind in my mortgage payments.

senses.def: When people or things fall to the ground from a higher position, it.! they fall down.
ex: I slipped on some ice on the sidewalk and fell down.

senses.def: When someone successfully tricks or deceives you, you fall for the trick or deception or you fall for it.
ex: I feel like an idiot. The salesman promised me it was a real diamond, not glass, and I fell for it.
Your girifriend told you that the guy she was dancing with at the party was her brother? How could you fall for a story like that?

senses.def: When you suddenly feel a strong attraction to someone or something, you fall for that person or thing.
ex: Jim met Sam's sister last week, and now he calls her every day. I guess he really fell for her in a big way.

senses.def: When people or things drop to a lower level from a higher place, they fall off the place where they were.
ex: The dish fell off the table and broke.
Be careful you don't fall off your bicycle.

senses.def: When the quality, degree, or frequency of something decreases, it falls off.
ex: Sales of fountain pens fell off after the ballpoint pen was invented.
The quality of his work has fallen off as he has gotten older.

related.def: A decrease in the quality, degree, or frequency of something is a falloff.
ex: The chairman was asked to explain the falloff in the company's sales.

senses.def: When you fall from or through something that is above ground level to the ground below, you fall out or fall out of it.
ex: Did he fall out or was he pushed?
I found a baby bird that had fallen out of its nest.
Michael fell out with his sister when he criticized her husband.
Melanie and Sarah started a company, but they fell out over who would be president and who would be vice-president.

related.def: When people have a falling-out, they become upset or angry with each other and no longer have friendly relations.

senses.def: When people or things fall over, they fall to the ground from an upright position.
ex: That tree has been dead for 50 years, but it still hasn't fallen over.

senses.def: When you fall over yourself or (usually) fall all over yourself, you try so hard to serve someone or to make someone like you that you appear foolish.
ex: The supervisor fell all over himself trying to satisfy the customer.
Mike was falling all over himself trying to impress Heather.
The soldiers fought back bravely, but the situation was hopeless.
After being accused of corruption, the senator said she would fight back and prove her innocence.

senses.def: When people or things drop through an opening from one side to the other side, they fall through.
ex: The roofer had fallen through a hole in the roof.
My Uncle Fred was ice fishing when he fell through a hole in the ice and was never seen again.

senses.def: When a plan, an arrangement, or a business deal does not happen or is canceled because of a problem or because someone does not do what is expected, it falls through.
ex: The family reunion fell through after Dad got sick.

forms: feel up to & feels up to

senses.def: When you feel up to doing something, you have the confidence or energy to do it.
ex: I'm sorry to cancel, but I just don't feel up to going dancing tonight.

senses.def: When you fight back an emotional response, such as tears or fear, you try very hard to overcome the emotion.
ex: The mother fought back tears when she saw the little white coffins.
I had to fight back ge to punch him in the nose.

senses.def: When you figure on something, you expect it or plan for it.
ex: I didn't figure on such cold weather. I wish I'd brought a coat.
You can figure on spending a least hundred bucks if you're going to that restaurant.

senses.def: When you fill in a form, you put information in the correct spaces. Fill out is the same as fill in.
ex: Maria filled in the job application and gave it to the secretary.
The teacher gave us the quiz and told us to fill the blanks in with the correct answers.

senses.def: When people want or need more information about a plan, situation, or occurrence and you supply that information, you fill them in.
ex: Something interesting happened while you were gone. I'll fill you in later.
I fell asleep during the meeting. Can you fill me in?

senses.def: When you temporarily do someone else's job, you fill in for that person.
ex: The regular bartender is on vacation, so Todd is filling in.
She's the star of the show.No one can fill in forher.

related.def: After you write all the information in the correct spaces of a form, the form is filled in.
ex: Are those forms blank or filled in?
This check isn't any good - the amount isn't filled in.

related.def: Someone who temporarily does someone else's job is a fill-in.
ex: Jerry is Ann's fill-in while she's on vacation.

senses.def: When you fill out a form, you put information in the correct spaces. Fill in is the same as fill out.
ex: The personnel director asked Sofia to fill out an application.
Fill the withdrawal slip out and give it to the bank teller.

senses.def: When slender people gain weight, they fill out.
ex: Jake was really thin when he got out of prison, but he has really filled out since then.
Nicole started to fill out after she started working at the candy shop.

related.def: After all the information is in the correct spaces of a form, the form is filled out.
ex: Here's my application. It's all filled out.
Are these forms blank or filled out?

senses.def: When you fill something up, you fillit completely.
ex: My radiator must be leaking. It has to be filled up with water every day.
We always fill the tank up when we're in Indiana because gas is cheaper there.

senses.def: When you fill up or fill up on something, you eat so much that you are no longer hungry and cannot eat any more.
ex: Don't fill up on salad - you won't have any room for dinner.
I filled up on candy and was really sick about an hour later.

senses.def: When a room or other area fills up, people enter it until it is full.
ex: The dance floor filled up quickly when the band began to play.
The hotels in Rio de Janeiro always fill up at carnival time.

related.def: After something has been completely filled up, it is filled up.
ex: These water containers don't weigh very much. Are you sure they're completely filled up?

senses.def: [not usually separated - the object can be a noun, a noun clause, or a complete sentence] When you find out information or a fact, you learn or become aware of that information or fact.
ex: If you don't know when the movie starts, look in the newspaper to find out.
I met a nice man at the party, but I never found out his name.
I met a nice man at the party, but I never found out what his name was.
I was surprised when I found out that he can speak 14 languages.
I was surprised when I found out he can speak 14 languages.

senses.def: When you fix up a place, such as a building, street, or park, you repair and decorate it.
ex: I am going to fix this place up and try to sell it.
The city decided to fix up the park.
Now that his house is fixed up, it looks pretty nice.
When you see how fixed up Jim's apartment is now, you'll be surprised.

senses.def: When you fix yourself up, you style your hair nicely and put on make-up and nice clothes.
ex: If you're going to that fancy restaurant, you'd better fix yourself up.
Heather is upstairs fixing herself up for the party.

senses.def: When you fix people up with something, you arrange for them to have or to use something that they need or want.
ex: We told the hotel desk clerk that we wanted their best room, and she fixed us up with the honeymoon suite.
The travel agent fixed me up with a limo to take me to the resort.

senses.label: informal
senses.def: When you fix people up or fix them up with someone, you arrange a date for them with a member of the opposite sex.
ex: Linda and Tom are perfect for each other. I'm going to fix them up.

related.label: informal
related.def: A fixer-upper is a building in poor condition that can be repaired, renovated, or redecorated in order to increase its value.
ex: The way to make money in real estate is to buy a fixer-upper and do as much of the work yourself as you can.

related.def: After you style your hair nicely and put on make-up and nice clothes, you are fixed up.
ex: Where's Lydia going? She's all fixed up.
I got all fixed up, and my boyfriend took me to a fast food restaurant.

senses.label: usually continuous
senses.def: When something is floating around a place,it is there somewhere, though you are not sure exactly where.
ex: The new schedule was floating around the office yesterday.

senses.def: When a rumor or some information is floating around, it is being repeated and discussed among a group of people or within a place.
ex: There's a rumor floating around that the factory's going to be closed.

senses.def: When you waste time playing or doing silly or unimportant things, you fool around. Goof around is the same as fool around.
ex: My son is lazy. He spends his time fooling around instead of looking for a job.
My boss said, "I'm not paying you to fool around - get to work!"

senses.def: When you fool around with something, you do something that may be dangerous or foolish.
ex: Fooling around with drugs is pretty stupid.
You shouldn't fool around with the insides of your computer unless you know what you're doing.

senses.label: informal
senses.def: When two people fool around or fool around with each other, they have sexual relations,even though one or both of them may be married to someone else or even though their families or society may not approve.
ex: Sally's father caught her and Jim fooling around in the basement.

senses.label: informal
senses.def: When you freak out, you become very upset or very angry. When you freak other people out, you cause them to become very upset or very angry.
ex: Melanie freaked out when she learned that her husband had been arrested for murder.

senses.def: When you get ahead, you become more successful and make progress in your job or your life.
ex: With your pessimistic attitude, you'll never get ahead.

senses.def: When you get along with people, you have peaceful, harmonious relations with them. Get on is similar to get along.
ex: Jim and his cousin aren't good friends, but they get along.
I haven't gotten along with my neighbors for years.

senses.def: When you are able to do some sort of work without any serious problems, you get along.
ex: How are you getting along in your new job?
Oh, I'm getting along OK, thank you.

senses.def: When you do something after waiting for some time because you are lazy, inefficient, or do not want to do it, you get around to it.
ex: I didn't get around to doing my taxes until April 14.

senses.def: When you escape from people who are chasing you because they want to hurt you or because you have committed a crime, you get away or get away from them.
ex: When he took the knife out of his pocket, I got away from him fast.
By the time the police arrived, the robbers had already gotten away.

senses.def: When you do something that is sneaky or wrong and you are not punished or criticized for it because no one knows or cares about it, you get away with it.
ex: Jake has been cheating on his taxes for years, and he always gets away with it.
He got away with stealing the money even though everyone knew he was guilty.

senses.def: When you get away from people or places, you leave them even though it may be difficult.
ex: I'm tired of this town. I need to get away.
Frank was talking and talking, and I couldn't get away from him.

senses.def: When you get away, you go on vacation.
ex: I have a lot of work to do, but I'll try to get away for a week or two.
We always try to get away in January and go skiing.

related.def: When you escape from people who want to capture or hurt you, you make a getaway.
ex: The robbers made their getaway in a blue Ford.
The car used for the getaway was found abandoned in the next town.

senses.def: When you return to a level or place where you were before, you get back or get back to that place.
ex: We left three weeks ago, and we didn't get back until yesterday.
Where are you going? Get right back here!
Mark lost a lot of weight when he was sick, and it took him a long time to get back to his old weight.

senses.def: When you get something back or get something back to a person or place, you return it to that person or place.
ex: Jim uses his mother's car in the morning, but she needs it to go to work at 4:30, so he has to get it back before then.
I have to get these books back to the library - they're overdue.

senses.def: When you get something back or get something back from someone or someplace, you have something that you had before.
ex: I couldn't believe I got my stolen car back.
Jim borrowed a book from me three years ago, and I still haven't gotten it back from him.

senses.def: When you get back or get back from something that is very hot or dangerous or that you should not be near, you move away from it so that there is more distance between you and it.
ex: Get back from the edge of the cliff! You might fall.
As the President came closer, the police told the crowd to get back.
Linda had some problems last semester, and she got behind in her studies.

senses.def: When you get back at people, you do something bad to them because they have done something bad to you.
ex: John won't forget what you did to him. He'll definitely get back at you someday.
She wants to get back at her ex-husband for the way he treated her.

senses.def: When you get back to people, you talk to them later, usually because you do not have time to talk to them at the time or because you will have information for them later that you do not have now.
ex: I don't have time to talk. now. I'm really busy. Can I get back to you?
That real estate agent still hasn't gotten back to me to let me know if our offer was accepted.

senses.def: When you get by or get by something, you pass something or someone while you are walking or driving even though it may be difficult because there is not enough room.
ex: Can you move all that junk in the hallway please? It's hard for people to get by.

senses.def: When you get by or get by on a certain amount of money, you phrasal verbs with get, part 1 continue with your work or continue with your life even though it may be difficult.
ex: Don't worry about me; I'll get by somehow.
It's not easy getting by on $250 a week.

senses.def: When something, such as a mistake or a problem, gets by you, you do not notice it.
ex: I've got a great editor. No mistakes get by her.
I checked this report twice. How did all these misspellings get by me?

senses.def: wWhen you move to a lower level or place or from north to south, you get down or get down to that level or place. Get up is the opposite of get down. Go down is similar to get down.
ex: You're going to fall out of that tree and break your neck. Get down right now!
The first thing I did after I got down to Miami was go to the beach.

senses.def: When you get things or people down, you move them from a higher level or place to a lower one.
ex: Why do you always put the dishes on the top shelf? I can't get them down.
The firefighters got the people down from the roof of the burning building.
When the enemy soldiers started shooting, the sergeant ordered his men to get down.
Get down! If the police catch us here we'll be in a lot of trouble.

senses.def: When things or people get you down, they make you sad or depressed.
ex: Don't let your troubles get you down. Everything will be all right.
Get in the car! We're going now.

senses.def: When a store gets something in, it receives a delivery of something that it will offer for sale.
ex: Karen asked the sales clerk when the store was going to get some summer dresses in.
I wanted to buy that new book, but the bookstore hasn't gotten it in yet.

senses.def: When you get an activity in, you find the time for it or make the time for it.
ex: Dinner isn't until 7:30, so we've got time to get a tennis game in.
Whenever I go to San Francisco on business, I try to get a baseball game in.

forms: phrasal verbs and can, could, wil, and would

senses.def: When you get off a bus, airplane, or train, you leave it.
ex: The bus stopped and I got off.
You can't get off the train while it's moving.

senses.def: When you are standing, lying, or sitting on something, such as a horse, bicycle, motorcycle, stage, platform, or piece of furniture, and you step down from it onto the ground, you get off it.
ex: You're so lazy. Why don't you get off the couch and help me?
Get off your bicycle and come inside.

senses.def: When you are standing within an area of ground, or on something that covers an area of ground, and you move to the side of it and step off of it, you get off it.
ex: The referee told the player to get off the field.
You're standing on our beach blanket - get off it!

senses.def: When you get something off, you remove it even though it may be difficult.
ex: I can't get this paint off my hands.
The top of this bottle is on so tight I cannot get it off.

senses.def: When you get a certain period of time off, you are allowed by your employer to miss work during this period.
ex: Pregnant women usually get three months off with pay.
Could I get tomorrow morning off to go to the doctor?

senses.def: When you get off, or get off work, you finish that day's work and leave your place of employment.
ex: Sally said she wouldn't get off work until 6:00.
I haven't gotten off early all week.

senses.def: When you do something wrong but are not punished, or you are punished only lightly for it, you get off. Someone who helps you to avoid punishment gets you off.
ex: He killed four people, but he got off with only three years in jail.
If his lawyer hadn't been so incompetent, he would have gotten him off with a lighter sentence.

senses.def: When you stop talking on the telephone, you get off the telephone.
ex: Get off the phone - I need to use it!

forms: get off on & gets off on

senses.def: [informal] When you get off on something or get off on doing something, you find it enjoyable and exciting.
ex: Sally loves winter sports, and she especially gets off on snowboarding.
Go away! I'm trying to study.
Mark went away not realizing he had left his briefcase behind.
We always go away for a few weeks in the winter.
Lydia is going to go away for a while.

senses.def: When you move your body toward something and stand, sit, or lie on it, you get on it.
ex: The nurse asked me to take off my shirt and get on the examination table.
If you get on that chair you can reach the top shelf.

senses.def: When you mount an animal, bicycle, motorcycle, and so on, you get on it.
ex: Getting on a camel isn't as easy as getting on a horse.
The children got back on their bikes and went home.

senses.def: When you enter a bus, train, airplane, ship, and so on, you get on it.
ex: The bus stopped so that I could get on.
Only people who are going on the cruise can get on the ship.

senses.def: When you get an item of clothing on, you put it on your body.
ex: Get your coat on. It's cold outside.
These gloves are too small. I can't get them on.

senses.def: When you continue doing something, you get on, get on with what you were doing, or get on with it.
ex: It's getting late. If we're going to finish this work today we'd better get on with it.

senses.def: When you get out or get out of a place, building, room, car, boat, and so on, you leave or escape from it.
ex: When Bob heard his car's engine making a strange noise, he got out and looked under the hood.
We smelled gas and got out of the building just seconds before it exploded.

senses.def: When you go to a place that is west of where you are or to a place outside a large city, you get out or get out to that place. ) i
ex: I love it here in the city. I almost never get out to the suburbs anymore.
I told my friend in New York, "If you ever get out to California, please visit me."

senses.def: When you get people out or get them out of a place, you take phrasal verbs with get, part 1 them out or you arrange for them to leave.
ex: The soldiers were surrounded, so they called for a helicopter to get them out.
After Hank was arrested, his lawyer got him out of jail.

senses.def: When you get out or get out of a dangerous, awkward, or difficult situation, you avoid it. When you get people out of a dangerous, awkward, or difficult situation, you help them to avoid it.
ex: Erik made a date with two girls for the same night. How is he going to get out of this mess?
You got me into this mess - you get me out!

senses.def: When you get something out or get something out of a container or place,you remove it.
ex: Mother's coming for dinner tonight, so let's get the good china out.
The videotape is jammed. I can't get it out of the VCR.

senses.def: When you get dirt or a stain out or get dirt or a stain out of a material, you remove it by cleaning.
ex: This detergent's ad claims it'll get dirt out even in cold water.
Do you think bleach will get this coffee stain out of my white blouse?

senses.def: When information gets out, it becomes known to people who are not supposed to know it.
ex: Be careful -- we'll be in a lot of trouble if this information gets out.
There was a huge scandal after the news got out.

senses.def: When you leave your house and do things that are relaxing and fun, you get out or get out of the house.
ex: You work too hard. You should get out more.
Ned doesn't get out of the house much. He prefers to stay home and play computergames.

senses.def: When you get out of something or get out of doing something you must do but do not want to do, you find a way to avoid it.
ex: Sam got out of gym class by pretending to be sick.
The boss wants me to work a double shift, but I'll get out of it.
I got out of going to church with my wife by pretending to be sick.

senses.def: If an activity gives you pleasure, satisfaction, or some other benefit, you get pleasure, satisfaction, or some other benefit out of it.
ex: I sat through that boring class for three months and didn't learn a thing. I didn't get anything out of it.
The judge didn't get any pleasure out of imposing such a harsh penalty.

senses.def: When you use force, pressure, or deceit to get something, such as information or money, from people, you get it out of them.
ex: They tortured him for days, but they couldn't get any information out of him.

senses.def: When you get over to a place, you go there. When you tell peo- ple to get over here, you want them to come where you are.
ex: Francisco called and he said he needs you to help him with something, so get over to his house right away.
Susie, get over here and clean up this mess immediately!

senses.def: When you get over a problem, illness, or emotionally painful experience, you stop letting it affect you and continue with your life. I've got a bad cold. I've been sick for a week, and I still haven't gotten over it. You can't feel sorry for yourself forever - you've got to get over it and get on with your life. and you cannot stop thinking about it, you cannot get over it. I can't get over seeing my ex-wife with her new husband. The coach couldn't get over losing the state championship 47 to 0.

senses.label: always separated
senses.def: When you want to get something over with, it is because it is something unpleasant that you want to finish so that you can stop worrying about it or dreading it.
ex: Let's fix both cavities today, doctor. I just want to get it over with.

senses.def: When you get through, get through with an activity, or get through doing an activity, you finish it or finish doing it.
ex: I have so much homework that I might not get through with it until midnight.
After you get through washing the dishes, you can start ironing.

senses.def: When you get through or get through to someone, usually on a telephone or radio, you are able to speak to that person.
ex: Nancy tried calling Jim last night, but she couldn't get through.
It wasn't easy, but I finally got through to my brother in Borneo.

senses.def: When you get through or get through to someone, you make that person understand your opinion or point of view.
ex: Mr. Taylor has tried to make his daughter understand why it's important to work hard in school and get good grades, but he just can't get through.
I've explained it a hundred times! What do I have to do to get through to you?

senses.label: informal
senses.def: When you get something through someone's head, you make that person understand your opinion or point of view. When you get something through your own head, you understand it.
ex: I finally got it through my son's head that / was serious about sending him to military school.
When are you going to get it through your head that our marriage is over?

senses.def: When something gets you through a difficult experience, it comforts and supports you.
ex: Julia's faith in God was what got her through the loss of her husband.
He was very nervous about giving the speech, so he had a drink to help get him through the ordeal.

senses.def: When you get to a place, you arrive there. When you get people to a place, you help them to go there or take them there. When you get to work, you arrive at the place where you work.
ex: Sarah left her house at 8:30 and got to the beach at 9:15.
When I get to Tokyo, I'll call to let you know I arrived safely.
Frank got fired because he kept getting to work late.
I went to the restaurant across the street for lunch, and I didn't get back to work until 2:30.

senses.def: When things or people get to a certain level, number, or amount, they reach it.
ex: It was very hot yesterday. It must have gotten to 100 degrees.
When I run, I always try to get to five miles before I quit.

senses.def: When you get to something that you want or need to do, you find the time to do it. When you get to work, you start working.
ex: I didn't have time to do the ironing last night. I'll try to get to it tonight.
Karen finally got back to her school project yesterday. She hadn't worked on it for weeks.
You've wasted the entire morning. When are you going to get to work?
My boss told me to get off the phone and get back to work.

senses.def: [informal] When you get to doing something, you begin to do it gradually.
ex: Dad got to thinking that maybe we ought to move to Los Angeles and try to find work there.
UFOs really exist after all.

senses.def: When you get to do something, you are allowed to do it or are able to do it.
ex: Timmy was excited because he got to ride a pony.
I hope I get to shake the President's hand after his speech.

senses.def: When something gets to you, it bothers or annoys you, either psychologically or physically.
ex: Jim's constant complaining is really starting to get to his wife.
Let's sit down and rest -- this heat is getting to me.

senses.def: When two people get together, they meet and spend time together. When you get together with someone, you meet and spend time with that person. ex: You should get all your tools together so you will have them when you need them.
Linda got all her tax records together to show to her accountant.

senses.def: [informal] When you get yourself together, or get it togeth- er, you gain control of your emotions after you have become upset or emotional.
ex: Bob was very upset before the party, but he got it together before the guests came.

ex: I'm having a little get-together tonight. Would you like to come?

senses.def: When you move to a higher level or place, or from south to north, you get up or get up to that level or place. Get down is the opposite of get up. Go up is similar to get up.
ex: Tom, your brother is in the basement. Please go tell him to get right up here and start doing his homework.

senses.def: When you get up or someone gets you up, you rise from your bed. When you get people up, you cause them to rise from their beds.
ex: I don't usually get up until 11:00 on weekends.
I make breakfast. Getting the children up and ready for school in the morning is Bil's job.

senses.def: When you change from a sitting or lying position to a standing position, you get up. Stand up is similar to get up.
ex: The teacher told the sleeping students to get up.

senses.def: When you give something away,you give it to someone without asking for anything in return because you do not want it or because you want to help the person you are giving it to.
ex: This old furniture isn't worth very much, so I think I'll just give it away.
He made nearly a billion dollars, but after he retired he gave most of his money away.

senses.def: When you give a secret away, you accidentally reveal that secret.
ex: I haven't seen that movie yet, so don't give away the ending.

senses.def: When you give yourself away, you accidentally reveal some- thing secret about yourself. When something gives you away, it accidentally reveals something secret about you.
ex: Mark tried to keep his affair a secret, but he was given away by his credit card bills.
Todd claimed he didn't care about Sally anymore, but he gave himself away when he asked who she had gone to the party with.

related.def: A giveaway is a statement or action that reveals secret information.

senses.def: When someone pressures or forces you to do something or allow some- thing even though you do not want to, you give in or give in to their request or demand.

senses.def: When you distribute something to other people, you give it out or give it out to them. Hand out is similar to give out.
ex: They gave out free hats to the first 5,ooo fans to enter the stadium.
The aid workers would have given more food out to the famine victims, but they didn't have enough.

senses.def: When a mechanical or electrical device stops working, it gives out or gives out on you. When a supply of something is completely used, it gives out or gives out on you.

senses.def: When you stop trying to do something because you think you will never succeed, you give up or give up on it.
ex: Forget it! This is impossible - I give up!
I've tried for years to have a nice looking lawn, but I've just given up on it.

senses.def: When you are running from or fighting with the police or enemy soldiers and you surrender, you give up or give yourself up.
ex: When the bank robbers realized they were surrounded by police, they gave up.
The suspect got tired of hiding from the police, and he gave himself up.

senses.def: When you stop doing something you do regularly, such as a sport or a job, you give it up.
ex: My father didn't give sky diving up until he was 82.
I had to give up my second job because I was so exhausted all the time.

senses.def: When you go about something or go about doing something, you begin or continue to follow all the steps necessary to do it.
ex: I have no idea how to go about opening a restaurant.

senses.def: When you chase and try to physically stop or to attack people, you go after them.

Captain Morgan was ordered to go after the enemy soldiers.

senses.def: When law enforcement officials try to prosecute people through a legal procedure, they go after them.
ex: Federal prosecutors are now going after the top drug dealers.
The senator introduced a bill designed to go after deadbeat dads.

senses.def: When a business tries to increase its profits by trying to increase its market share or its number of customers, it goes after them. The tobacco company denied going after the teenage market. The CEO said he wanted to go after new customers in China.

ex: Sofia went after a degree in accounting.
Todd trained for a year before going after the record in the 100-yard dash.

ex: I've decided to go ahead with my plan to reorganize the company.

ex: What are you waiting for? Go ahead.

senses.def: When you agree with people or agree with what they are saying, you go along with them.

senses.def: When people or things follow a circular path and return to the same place, they go around.

senses.def: When people or things follow an indirect or curved path in order to avoid an obstacle or to change direction, they go around or go around the obstacle.

There was some broken glass in the street, but I went around it.

senses.def: When an object spins or turns, it goes around.

The children have to stay on the merry-go-round until it stops going around.

senses.def: When you go around a place, you visit various parts of it.
ex: The president went around the state giving the same speech at every stop.
The exterminator is going around the house looking for rats.

senses.def: When you go around in a certain condition or go around doing something, you go to various places and allow other people see you.
ex: I was so embarrassed - / went around all day with my zipper open.
Are you going to go around all day wearing that stupid hat?

senses.def: When you go around doing something, you go to various places and deliberately do something that may bother or upset other people.
ex: The new manager goes around telling everyone how to do their jobs.
Don't go around sticking your nose in other people's business.

senses.def: When something goes around, it spreads to various parts of a larger place.
ex: A rumor went around that the plant was going to close.
He probably has the flu. It's been going around.

senses.def: When something is being distributed to a group of people and there is enough for everyone, there is enough to go around.
ex: There wasn't enough food to go around, and some of the famine victims got nothing.
Don't make the pieces of wedding cake too big, otherwise there won't be enough to go around.

senses.def: When you leave your home and live temporarily at another place, such as a school, you go away to that place.
ex: Jane didn't go away to school. She went to a school near her home.
Some young people are nervous about going away to school, but others look forward to it.

senses.def: When a condition, problem, situation, or activity disappears or greatly decreases,it goes away.
ex: I have a pain in my back that never goes away.
If the rain doesn't go away, we'll have to call off the game.

senses.def: When a condition, problem, practice, or custom goes back to a certain time, it began at that time.
ex: The tradition of saluting in the military goes back to the Middle Ages.
His drug problem goes back to his college years.

senses.def: When you are discussing the age of something, you go back or go back to when it was created or started.
ex: This table is very valuable. It goes back to the 1760s.

ex: I promised to take my son to a baseball game, and I'm not going back on my word.
The President went back on his pledge not to raise taxes.

senses.def: When people or things are better or worse, or do something in a better or worse way than is normal or expected, they go beyond what is normal or expected.
ex: Did you say Jackson's new book is good? I think it goes beyond good - it's fantastic!

senses.def: When people go by a place or thing, they pass near that place or thing. When a thing goes by or goes by you, it passes near you.

I went by Jim's house to see if his car was in the driveway.

senses.def: When you go by a place, you go there so that you can do something or get something.
ex: Let's go by Raul's house to get his tools before we work on your car.
You can forget about going by the dry cleaner to pick up your stuff - it's closed.

senses.def: When a period of time goes by, it passes.
ex: I can't believe that 30 years have gone by since I got out of high school.
As time went by, Betty moved up in the company until she was the head of the finance department.

senses.def: When you go by a policy or standard, you use it as a reference or a guide in making decisions and determining your behavior. When you go by the book, you follow rules, policies, or laws exactly.
ex: Going by the book has always been my policy.

Don't go by the clock on the wall. It's fast. Go by the clock on the desk.
No wonder I'm always late for work -- the clock I've been going by is ten minutes slow.

senses.def: When you move to a lower level or position or from north to south, you go down or go down to that place. Go up is the opposite of go down.
ex: Going down the mountain was a lot easier than going up.

senses.def: When the cost, rate, quality, quantity, or level of something decreases, it goes down. Go up is the opposite of go down.
ex: The temperature went down to zero last night.
The crime rate in New York City has gone down.

senses.def: When something extends to a certain point that is farther south or at a lower elevation, it goes down to that point. Go up is the opposite of go down.
ex: How far south does this road go down?
Does this road go down to the south side of town?
After dinner we went down to the basement and played ping pong.

senses.def: When something goes down in a certain way, people react to or perceive it in this way.
ex: The new no smoking policy didn't go down very well with the smokers in the office.
The judge's decision went down well with the prosecutor.

senses.def: When a computer or computer network stops working because of a problem or because it has been disconnected, it goes down.
ex: I couldn't withdraw any money at the bank because its computers had gone down.
If your computer terminal goes down, you can use the one in the next office.

senses.def: When the sun goes below the horizon, it goes down.
ex: After the sun goes down, it'll get a little cooler.
The sun went down at 8:34 last night.

senses.def: When an electrical device or system goes off,it stops operating. Come on is the opposite of go off.

A thermostat makes the air conditioner go off if it gets below a certain temperature.

senses.def: When you go off, you leave a place or the people you are with and go to a different place. When you go off with someone, you leave a place or the people you are with and go to a different place with them.

senses.def: When an event or plan goes off well, smoothly, without a problem, or without a hitch (a hitch is a problem),it happens as planned.
ex: The wedding went off without a hitch.
The invasion didn't go off the way the general planned it.

senses.def: When a road, trail, path, and so on, goes off, it leaves the main road, trail, or path, and goes in a different direction.
ex: This trail that goes off to the left will take you to the campground.

senses.def: When an electrical device or system goes on, it begins to operate.
ex: A thermostat makes the air conditioner go on if it gets above a certain temperature.

I told him to stop talking, but he went on and on and on and on.

senses.def: When an event or activity goes on, it continues.
ex: The party went on until dawn.

senses.def: When an electrical light goes out, it stops producing light because it is no longer receiving power.

When the old tree fell on the power lines, every light in town went out.

senses.def: When two people with a romantic interest in each other go out, they go together to a place of entertainment in order to have fun and spend time together.

senses.def: When you carefully explain something, usually something that is complicated but important, you go over it.

The singer's performance went over well with the critics.
